docs.title: Native (experimental)
docs.text: A planning backend whose work happens in a compiled core (Rust) inside the Python process: no Docker, no PyBullet, no ROS. It is experimental: the API is the usual compas_fab backend API, but what it supports is limited (see below) and may change.

docs.title: When to use
docs.text:
• Cartesian paths (lines, spirals, toolpaths), fast: frame or point-axis waypoints, for 6-axis arms, redundant arms and robots on external axes.
  • Free motion between configurations, frames or point-axis targets, around obstacles.
  • Inverse kinematics for any serial robot: closed form where there is one, numerical otherwise.
  • Checking many configurations for collisions at once.
  • Obstacles with holes or concave shapes, through distance fields.
  • Trying it out and telling us what breaks.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text: What you get What you give up Cartesian paths in milliseconds, through the compas_fab API Robots without a closed form search a beam of postures along the path (8 by default, tracks): wide, but not exhaustive Free motion in milliseconds, for any serial robot, timed under velocity and acceleration limits No jerk limits yet Closed-form IK for UR (offset wrist) and spherical-wrist arms; numerical IK (collision-aware) for every other robot Numerical IK finds solutions from seeds: "no solution" means none was found, not that none exists Sphere-model collision checks for thousands of configurations per millisecond, validated on exact meshes, including tools and workpieces the robot carries Large flat links (gantry carriages, tall bases) are approximated poorly by spheres (planner.poorly_fitted_links); the exact check catches what the spheres miss, at the cost of slower plans (exact_links checks them during planning too, slower still) Mesh obstacles with holes (distance fields) Experimental: the API may change between minor versions

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
pip install compas_fab_native

Wheels are available for Linux (x86_64), macOS (Intel and Apple Silicon) and Windows (x64), for Python 3.9 and later. Elsewhere, pip builds the extension from source, which needs a Rust toolchain. From a checkout of the repository, pip install -e . builds it in place.

docs.title: First example
docs.text:
Forward and inverse kinematics on a UR5:

"""01 - Forward and inverse kinematics with the native planner.

The native planner is a compas_fab backend like any other: you give it a RobotCell, then
ask it for kinematics, collision checks and paths. The difference is underneath: the work
happens in a compiled (Rust) core instead of Python, PyBullet or ROS.

Install the core once with ``pip install .`` from a compas_fab checkout.
"""

import time

from compas.geometry import Frame
from compas_fab.backends import UR5Kinematics
from compas_fab.robots import FrameTarget
from compas_fab.robots import RobotCellLibrary
from compas_fab.robots import TargetMode

from compas_fab_native import NativePlanner

# 1. A robot cell: a UR5 on its own. `state` holds everything that moves: the robot's joint
#    values, its base frame, tools and obstacles.
robot_cell, state = RobotCellLibrary.ur5()

# 2. The planner. A UR has an offset wrist, so we tell it which closed-form solver to use.
#    (Spherical-wrist arms like ABB or Staubli need nothing: the solver is derived from the
#    robot model.) `set_robot_cell` sends the robot to the core, fitting collision spheres
#    to every link mesh. That takes a moment, once.
planner = NativePlanner(UR5Kinematics())
t0 = time.perf_counter()
planner.set_robot_cell(robot_cell, state)
print("set_robot_cell: {:.0f} ms (once per cell)".format((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1e3))

# 3. Forward kinematics: where is the flange (the robot coordinate frame, RCF) for these joints?
state.robot_configuration.joint_values = [0.0, -1.2, 1.4, -1.8, -1.57, 0.0]
flange = planner.forward_kinematics(state, TargetMode.ROBOT)
print("flange at", flange.point)

# 4. Inverse kinematics: every way the robot can reach a frame. A 6-axis arm has up to 8
#    (shoulder left/right x elbow up/down x wrist flip). Collision checking is on by default,
#    so solutions where the robot hits itself or an obstacle are dropped.
target = FrameTarget(Frame([0.4, 0.2, 0.5], [1, 0, 0], [0, -1, 0]), TargetMode.ROBOT)
solutions = list(planner.iter_inverse_kinematics(target, state))
print("{} collision-free IK solutions".format(len(solutions)))
for configuration in solutions:
    print("  ", ["{:+.2f}".format(v) for v in configuration.joint_values])

# 5. How fast? Time many IK calls, including the collision check of every solution.
n = 200
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(n):
    list(planner.iter_inverse_kinematics(target, state))
print("IK + collision check: {:.0f} us per target (mostly Python overhead)".format((time.perf_counter() - t0) / n * 1e6))

docs.title: More examples
docs.text:
Each example builds on the previous one and explains what the planner does as it goes.

  • 02_collision_checking.py: the sphere model, checking 10,000 configurations at once, and how spheres compare with exact meshes
  • 03_cartesian_line.py: a 100-waypoint line, what the planner does, and starting from the current configuration
  • 04_tool_and_free_axis.py: a spiral toolpath that only works when the tool may turn about its own axis
  • 05_mesh_obstacles.py: plunging through a ring, impossible with bounding boxes, possible with a distance field
  • 06_free_motion.py: free motion around obstacles, to configurations, frames and point-axis targets, timed under the joint limits, on a UR5 and a 7-axis Panda

docs.title: How it works, in short
docs.text:
The full explanation, with diagrams, is in How it works.

  1. set_robot_cell fits spheres inside every link mesh and sends the robot, its meshes and the obstacles to the core. Sphere fits are cached (in memory and in ~/.cache/compas_fab/native_spheres; COMPAS_FAB_NATIVE_CACHE=0 turns that off), so setting up the same cell again takes milliseconds. Tools and workpieces the planning group carries get spheres on the link that carries them; everything that stands still while it plans (other robots of the cell, their tools, parked tools) becomes an obstacle.
  2. IK is closed-form where possible: ported for UR arms, derived from the model for spherical-wrist arms. Other robots (a 7-axis arm, a robot on a gantry) get numerical IK: a least-squares solve that also keeps the robot clear of collisions. options={"ik": "numeric"} uses it for any robot.
  3. A Cartesian request first fills in frames between the waypoints (every max_step, 1 cm by default, and max_step_angle, 0.1 rad), so the tool moves in straight lines. With closed-form IK it solves every frame (and every sampled rotation about the tool axis), checks all solutions for collisions in one batch, and searches for the smoothest sequence through them. With numerical IK it carries a beam of postures along the path, branching into new ones when they die out, and picks the smoothest sequence. Point-axis waypoints leave the rotation about the axis free.
  4. The chosen path is validated on the exact meshes; if a configuration collides there, the search continues without it.
  5. Free motion tries the straight joint-space motion first, then RRT-Connect from the start and from every goal at once, then shortcutting and smoothing, and checks the result on the exact meshes (if it touches them, it plans again with a safety margin). Its collision checks run 8 configurations at a time in SIMD and stop at the first contact.
  6. The path is then timed: corners are rounded off within a tolerance (if the rounded corner is collision-free), and the speed along the path is the fastest the joint velocity and acceleration limits allow, starting and ending at rest.

Design notes, measurements and open issues are in SPIKE.md.

docs.text: See the API reference.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text: compas_fab_native is a compas_fab backend: you use it through the regular compas_fab planner API (set_robot_cell, inverse_kinematics, check_collision, plan_cartesian_motion, plan_motion, ...). The pages of compas_fab document those calls; this page covers what is specific to the native backend: its constructor options and the planner options it understands.

docs.title: compas_fab_native.NativePlanner
docs.text:
NativePlanner(kinematics_solver=None, sphere_options: Optional[dict] = None, exact: bool = True, obstacles: str = 'boxes', esdf_options: Optional[dict] = None, exact_links=None)

Bases: SetRobotCell, SetRobotCellState, ForwardKinematics, InverseKinematics, CheckCollision, PlanCartesianMotion, PlanMotion, PlannerInterface

Planner backed by the native (Rust) motion core.

Parameters:

  • kinematics_solver –

    compas_fab analytical solver of the robot (e.g. UR5Kinematics()); its parameters are handed to the core's closed-form IK.

  • sphere_options (Optional[dict], default: None ) –

    Sphere fitting options (see model.fit_sphere_sets).

  • exact (bool, default: True ) –

    Keep the exact collision meshes in the core. Planned Cartesian paths are then validated on the meshes (parry3d) after the sphere search, and the search continues until the path is collision-free under both models. Default True.

  • obstacles (str, default: 'boxes' ) –

    How the sphere search sees static rigid bodies: "boxes" (oriented bounding boxes, default) or "esdf" (a signed distance field of their meshes; bodies with touch links, like a floor, stay boxes).

  • esdf_options (Optional[dict], default: None ) –

    voxel (0.02 m), truncation (0.3 m) and margin (0.01 m) of the ESDF.

  • exact_links –

    Links to check on their exact geometry inside planning too, not only in the final exact check: None (default), "auto" (the links spheres represent poorly, see poorly_fitted_links) or a list of link names. They are tested as convex hulls (conservative) against each other and the scene's boxes, on every configuration the spheres find free. Useful when the final check keeps rejecting paths near large flat links (a gantry carriage); it slows planning down, and the hulls take free space away. Needs exact=True.

docs.title: poorly_fitted_links property
docs.text:
poorly_fitted_links

Links whose collision spheres miss their mesh by more than model.EXACT_LINK_MISS (95th percentile): the spheres cannot represent them (a gantry carriage, a tall base), so collisions with them are only caught by the exact check. See the exact_links option.

docs.title: check_collision
docs.text:
check_collision(robot_cell_state, options=None)

Collision check on the sphere model, or on the exact meshes with options["exact"].

docs.title: iter_inverse_kinematics
docs.text:
iter_inverse_kinematics(target, robot_cell_state=None, group=None, options=None)

IK solutions of a FrameTarget or PointAxisTarget, collision-free unless options["check_collision"] is False.

Robots with a closed form (kinematics_solver, or a spherical wrist the core derives one for) get all of its solutions; for a PointAxisTarget, those of axis_samples rotations about the axis. Other robots (redundant arms, external axes) use the core's numerical IK, which treats the rotation about a point-axis target's axis as free.

Options

check_collision : bool Only collision-free solutions (sphere model). Default True. ik : str "auto" (default: closed form if there is one), "numeric" or "analytic". max_results : int Numerical IK: distinct solutions at most. Default 8. seed : int Numerical IK: offset of the random seeds. Default 0. The state's configuration is always tried first. axis_samples : int Closed form, point-axis targets: rotations sampled about the axis. Default 16.

docs.title: plan_cartesian_motion
docs.text:
plan_cartesian_motion(waypoints, start_state, group=None, options=None)

Cartesian path through FrameWaypoints or PointAxisWaypoints.

The tool moves in straight lines between waypoints: frames are interpolated every max_step metres and max_step_angle radians (like MoveIt and PyBullet), and the trajectory has one point per interpolated frame, passing through every waypoint.

Robots with a closed form plan over all IK branches at once (layered graph search). Other robots (redundant arms, external axes) follow the path with numerical IK from several starting solutions and keep the cheapest that stays collision-free. Point-axis waypoints leave the rotation about the axis free: continuously with numerical IK, sampled (free_axis_samples) with the closed form.

Options

max_step : float Largest distance between interpolated frames, metres. Default 0.01. 0 or None: the waypoints only. max_step_distance is accepted as an alias. max_step_angle : float Largest rotation between interpolated frames, radians. Default 0.1. free_axis_samples : int Closed form: rotations about the tool axis sampled per waypoint. Default 1 for frame waypoints (the frames as given), 16 for point-axis waypoints. free_axis_range : float Half-range of that rotation in radians. Default pi. ik : str "auto" (default: closed form if there is one), "numeric" or "analytic". tracks : int Numerical IK: starting solutions followed along the path. Default 8. seed : int Numerical IK: offset of the random seeds. Default 0. max_joint_step : float Largest joint change between consecutive frames (rad, or m for prismatic joints). Default 0.5. start_from_state : bool Begin the path at start_state's configuration. Default False (any IK branch). exact_check : bool Validate the path on the exact meshes (needs NativePlanner(exact=True)). Default True.

docs.title: plan_motion
docs.text:
plan_motion(target, start_state, group=None, options=None)

Collision-free joint-space motion from start_state to target.

The straight joint-space motion is tried first, then RRT-Connect from the start and from every goal at once, then shortcutting and B-spline smoothing. The result is checked on the exact meshes and re-planned with another seed if it touches them.

Targets

ConfigurationTarget One goal. FrameTarget Every IK solution is a goal; the planner picks whichever it reaches. PointAxisTarget IK solutions of axis_samples rotations about the axis.

Options

range : float Longest tree extension, in joint-space distance. Default 1.0. resolution : float Collision checks per unit of joint-space distance. Default: enough that no robot sphere moves more than about 2 cm between checks (core.default_resolution). max_iterations : int Default 100000. seed : int Sampling sequence offset, for different (reproducible) paths. Default 0. simplify : bool Shortcut and smooth the path. Default True. exact_check : bool Validate the path on the exact meshes. Default True. exact_step : float Largest joint change between exact checks (rad). Default 0.02. axis_samples : int Rotations sampled about a PointAxisTarget's axis. Default 16. time_parameterization : bool Time the path under joint velocity and acceleration limits (TOPP-RA), with blended corners, starting and ending at rest. Points then carry time_from_start, velocities and accelerations. Default True. velocity_scaling, acceleration_scaling : float Fractions of the limits to use. Default 1.0. max_acceleration : float or list Joint acceleration limits (URDFs carry none). Default: twice each joint's velocity limit, i.e. full speed in half a second. blend_tolerance : float Largest joint-space deviation of a blended corner from the planned path. Blends that collide shrink, down to a stop at that corner. Default 0.05. time_step : float Sampling period of the timed trajectory in seconds. Default 0.01. max_joint_step : float Without time parameterization: interpolate the path so no joint moves more than this between points. Default: the path's vertices only.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• NativePlanner and NativeClient: a compas_fab planning backend on a compiled (Rust) core, moved here from the compas_fab spike branch with its history.
  • Forward kinematics, and inverse kinematics for frame and point-axis targets: closed form for UR arms and spherical-wrist arms (derived from the robot model), numerical and collision-aware for any other serial robot.
  • check_collision on the sphere model or on the exact meshes, including tools and workpieces the robot carries.
  • plan_cartesian_motion for frame and point-axis waypoints in robot, tool and workpiece mode, with free rotation about the tool axis.
  • plan_motion to configuration, frame and point-axis targets, timed under joint velocity and acceleration limits.
  • Mesh obstacles as signed distance fields (NativePlanner(obstacles="esdf")), which keep holes and concave shapes open.
  • Release workflow on compas-dev/compas-actions: wheels for Linux (x86_64), macOS (universal2) and Windows (x64), each tested on Python 3.9 and 3.13, a source distribution, and publishing to PyPI.
  • License texts of the Rust crates compiled into the extension, in licenses/THIRD_PARTY_RUST.txt.
  • Documentation site.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • Collision spheres are fitted in the core instead of in Python with trimesh: about 20 times faster (0.08 s instead of 1.7 s to set up a UR5), and trimesh and rtree are no longer dependencies.

docs.title: How the native backend works
docs.text:
This page explains what the native backend does internally: which parts exist, what happens when you call it, and why it is built that way. It is written for people who maintain or extend it. For using it, see Native (experimental).

The diagrams are generated by docs/diagrams/build.py. Click one to open it full size.

docs.title: The big picture
docs.text:
The backend has two halves.

Python (src/compas_fab_native/) translates between compas_fab and the core:

  • planner.py holds NativePlanner, which implements the compas_fab backend features (SetRobotCell, InverseKinematics, PlanMotion, …). It converts targets, waypoints and target modes (robot, tool, workpiece) into frames of the robot's end-effector link in robot coordinates, calls the core, and turns its results into compas_fab objects (Configuration, JointTrajectory).
  • model.py describes a RobotCell in the form the core needs: a kinematic tree, collision spheres, obstacle boxes and meshes. This is where the geometry work happens (sphere fitting, bounding boxes, which links move and which do not).

Rust (crates/) does the numeric work:

  • motion_py is the Python extension (compas_fab_native.NativeCore). It holds one robot and its scene, and releases the GIL while it works. Robots and scenes cross the boundary as JSON; frames as flat lists of 12 numbers (a 3×4 matrix, row-major).
  • motion_core is the planner proper: forward kinematics, the collision checkers, IK, the Cartesian and free-space planners, and time parameterization.
  • motion_exact checks configurations on the exact collision meshes (with parry3d).
  • motion_gpu runs the same collision queries on the GPU. Only the benchmarks use it.

A call such as plan_motion goes: NativePlanner → NativeCore.plan_motion → motion_core::freespace::plan, with motion_exact validating the result.

docs.title: Setting up a cell
docs.text:
set_robot_cell(cell, state, options={"group": ...}) builds the robot description once. set_robot_cell_state then updates the core whenever the state changes.

  1. Split by planning group (model.planning_links). The core plans one group, such as the UR5's manipulator or the RFL's robot11_eaXYZ (a gantry and an arm, 9 joints). Links that the group's joints move form the core's kinematic tree. Every other link becomes a static obstacle posed at the state's configuration: in the RFL that is the other bridge, its robots, the rails and the hall. The core takes at most 32 links, and this split is what keeps large cells within that limit. A single robot is described whole, exactly as before the split existed.
  2. Carried objects (model.carried_objects): the tool attached to the group, rigid bodies attached to that tool (a workpiece in the gripper), and rigid bodies attached to links the group moves. They get spheres on the link that carries them, and collisions with their touch links are disabled.
  3. Everything else (model.static_obstacles, plus free rigid bodies) becomes obstacles:
  4. static links;
  5. tools on other groups and what they hold;
  6. bodies attached to links the group cannot move;
  7. parked tools.

Obstacles reach the core as oriented boxes (obstacle_boxes, the smallest of a few candidate boxes), or, with NativePlanner(obstacles="esdf"), as a signed distance field built from their meshes, which keeps holes and concave shapes open. 4. Sphere fit (model.fit_sphere_sets, which runs in the core: motion_exact::spheres). Each link gets two sets: - self-collision spheres, inscribed in the mesh (spheres around neighbouring links would overlap permanently); - obstacle spheres, the same spheres grown by 2 cm.

Fits are scored by how far the surface reaches outside the spheres (miss). Links without a closed mesh get spheres that enclose clusters of surface points instead. They're cached in memory and on disk, keyed by the mesh and the options, so setting up the same cell again takes milliseconds (cached_sphere_sets). 5. Exact meshes: every link and obstacle mesh also goes to motion_exact.

When the state changes, three things can happen, keyed in set_robot_cell_state:

  • Attachments changed (_attachment_key): the robot's own spheres change, so the core is rebuilt.
  • Obstacles changed (scene_key, including touch links): only the scene is replaced (NativeCore.set_scene).
  • Joints outside the group moved (a gripper's fingers, mimic joints): those values are folded into the joint origins (set_passive_joints).

When the core is built it also samples 1,000 random configurations. Link pairs whose spheres overlap in 95% of them are treated like SRDF-disabled pairs, as MoveIt does for pairs that are "always in collision". The same is done for spheres that always touch an obstacle box, such as a base standing on the floor.

docs.title: The collision model
docs.text:
Planning needs millions of collision checks, and exactness is only needed at the end. So the backend checks in layers:

  1. Broad phase: each link has a bounding sphere around its spheres. A link whose bounding sphere is clear of everything is skipped as a whole.
  2. Spheres: link spheres against obstacle boxes, the ESDF and other links' spheres. There are two implementations:
  3. motion_core::check::Checker answers yes or no. RRT, motion checks and timing use it. It runs 4 configurations at once (8 on x86) in SIMD and stops at the first contact, following VAMP's design.
  4. motion_core::cpu::collision_min_lanes returns clearances, the smallest distance in metres. IK, the Cartesian planners and check_collision use it.
  5. Convex hulls (opt-in): NativePlanner(exact_links="auto") also checks the links that spheres represent poorly on every configuration the spheres pass, as convex hulls with a 5 mm margin (ExactChecker::check_focus). planner.poorly_fitted_links lists those links: gantry carriages, tall bases.
  6. Exact meshes (ExactChecker::check): parry3d mesh-against-mesh tests. They decide what is handed out. Goals of plan_motion that touch the meshes are dropped, and every planned path is checked along its length. A path that fails is planned again.

Sphere accuracy, measured with fit_miss at the 95th percentile:

Robot Miss UR5, Panda 1–2 cm ABB IRB 4600 6.5–9 cm RFL carriages 0.4–0.6 m RFL bridge up to 1.4 m

The exact check makes the result correct either way, but the more the spheres miss, the more plans get rejected and redone. Boxes as robot-side primitives are the open fix (see SPIKE.md).

Touch links work as in compas_fab: an obstacle or carried object lists the links that may touch it. Each check skips those pairs: spheres, hulls and meshes alike.

docs.title: Inverse kinematics
docs.text:
The core picks the IK per robot:

  • Closed form (motion_core::ik): a port of ROS-Industrial's ur_kinematics for UR arms, and a solver derived from the model for 6-axis arms with a spherical wrist (ABB, Stäubli, KUKA-like). It returns every solution within the joint limits.
  • Numerical (motion_core::numik), for every other robot: 7-axis arms, robots on external axes. options={"ik": "numeric"} uses it for any robot.

Numerical IK solves one weighted least-squares problem per seed, after PyRoki's formulation:

  • Pose: the TCP position and its rotation. For a point-axis target, only the direction of the tool axis counts, so the rotation about it is free.
  • Rest pull: a weak pull towards the seed's posture. It only steers the joints a redundant arm can move without moving the TCP, and it is dropped near the target so it never bends the result.
  • Collisions: obstacle spheres within 1 cm of an obstacle, and self-collision sphere pairs within 1 cm of each other. Near the target the margin drops to zero, so only real contacts count.

Jacobians are written out: the geometric Jacobian of the chain, and the sphere distance gradients the checker already has. Joint limits are kept by clamping every step.

Robots with prismatic joints (gantries, rails) first go through a carry stage. It moves only those joints, so the TCP reaches the target with the seed's arm posture. Without it, a random seed on a 37 m rail would leave the arm stretching for a target metres away.

Seeds are the caller's first (for example the current configuration), then random ones, solved in parallel. Solutions are kept if the pose converged, nothing touches, the checker accepts them, and they differ from the ones already found.

docs.title: Free motion: plan_motion
docs.text:
1. Goals.
  2. A configuration target is its own goal.
  3. A frame target becomes every IK solution.
  4. A point-axis target becomes the solutions over rotations about the axis: sampled for the closed form, continuous for numerical IK.

Goals that touch the exact meshes are dropped first, because every path to them would fail the final check. 2. Straight motion. If the joint-space line from the start to a goal is free, that's the path. 3. RRT-Connect (motion_core::freespace) grows trees from the start and from every goal at once, with VAMP's dynamic domain and tree balancing. The path is then shortened and smoothed with B-splines. 4. Exact check along the path, every 0.02 rad. If the path touches, the planner re-plans with spheres inflated by 5, 10, 20 and 30 mm. Inflating keeps it from finding the same grazing path again; a new seed alone would not. 5. Timing (motion_core::timing). Corners are rounded off within blend_tolerance where the rounded corner is free. Speeds come from TOPP-RA: the fastest motion within the joint velocity and acceleration limits, starting and ending at rest.

docs.title: Cartesian paths: plan_cartesian_motion
docs.text:
1. Fill in frames. Frames are added between waypoints every max_step (1 cm) and max_step_angle (0.1 rad), so the tool moves in straight lines. max_step: 0 keeps only the given waypoints.
  2. Closed-form robots (cartesian::plan_cartesian_with). Every frame, rotated about the tool axis free_axis_samples times, gets all its IK solutions: one layer per frame. All solutions are collision-checked in one batch, and dynamic programming finds the path through the layers with the least joint motion. No joint may move more than max_joint_step between frames.
  3. Other robots (cartesian::plan_cartesian_tracked), a beam search:
  4. Each frame keeps up to tracks (8) configurations, each solved from one of the previous frame's, using it as both seed and rest posture so the joints move as little as possible.
  5. When fewer than a quarter survive (collisions, joint limits, a lost target), the search branches from perturbed postures.
  6. The path is then the cheapest through the layers, as in step 2.
  7. Lazy checks in both planners. The motion along the chosen path is checked: on the spheres, then on the exact meshes. Failing edges and nodes are blocked and the search runs again, until a path passes or none is left.

This repository contains code ported from, data derived from, and algorithms that closely

2. VAMP: Vector-Accelerated Motion Planning
   https://github.com/KavrakiLab/vamp
   Authors: Zachary Kingston, Wil Thomason, Clayton Ramsey and contributors (Kavraki Lab).
   License: Apache-2.0 (licenses/Apache-2.0.txt)
   W. Thomason, Z. Kingston, L. E. Kavraki, "Motions in Microseconds via Vectorized
   Sampling-Based Planning", ICRA 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.14545

   Used in:
   - crates/motion_core/src/freespace.rs: RRT-Connect with dynamic domain and tree
     balancing, the Halton sampler bases, and the shortcut and B-spline simplification
     follow VAMP's `planning/rrtc.hh`, `planning/simplify.hh`, `random/halton.hh` and their
     default settings (`rrtc_settings.hh`, `simplify_settings.hh`). Rewritten in Rust;
     modified: f32 node storage per tree, multi-goal handling, no allocations per iteration.
   - crates/motion_core/src/check.rs: the motion check "rake" of `planning/validate.hh`
     (lanes spread over the motion, stepping back together), the sphere/cuboid test of
     `collision/sphere_cuboid.hh`, link bounding spheres before link spheres, and early exit.
     Rewritten in Rust on `wide` SIMD vectors.
   - fixtures/vamp_panda.json, fixtures/vamp_ur5.json: kinematic trees, collision spheres
     and disabled pairs converted from VAMP's `resources/panda/panda_spherized.urdf`,
     `panda.srdf`, `resources/ur5/ur5_spherized.urdf` and `ur5.srdf`
     (scripts/export_vamp_robot.py).
   - crates/motion_bench/src/mbm.rs: VAMP's rules for turning MotionBenchMaker problems into
     obstacles (`problem_dict_to_vamp`). The problems themselves are not included.

5. MotionBenchMaker
   C. Chamzas, C. Quintero-Peña, Z. Kingston, A. Orthey, D. Rakita, M. Gleicher,
   M. Toussaint, L. E. Kavraki, "MotionBenchMaker: A Tool to Generate and Benchmark Motion

   The benchmark problems used in SPIKE.md and results/mbm_m3max.md (as shipped by VAMP).

6. Algorithms implemented from publications (no code taken)
   - crates/motion_core/src/timing.rs, path with circular blends: T. Kunz, M. Stilman,
     "Time-Optimal Trajectory Generation for Path Following with Bounded Acceleration and
     Velocity", Robotics: Science and Systems 2012.
   - crates/motion_core/src/timing.rs, time parameterization: H. Pham, Q.-C. Pham, "A New
     Approach to Time-Optimal Path Parameterization Based on Reachability Analysis", IEEE
     Transactions on Robotics 34(3), 2018.
   - crates/motion_core/src/freespace.rs: J. J. Kuffner, S. M. LaValle, "RRT-Connect: An
     Efficient Approach to Single-Query Path Planning", ICRA 2000; dynamic domain:
     A. Yershova, L. Jaillet, T. Siméon, S. M. LaValle, "Dynamic-Domain RRTs", ICRA 2005.
   - crates/motion_core/src/ik.rs, spherical wrist: product of exponentials and the
     Paden-Kahan subproblems (R. M. Murray, Z. Li, S. S. Sastry, "A Mathematical
     Introduction to Robotic Manipulation", CRC Press 1994).
   - crates/motion_core/src/numik.rs, numerical IK: Levenberg-Marquardt (K. Levenberg, "A
     Method for the Solution of Certain Non-Linear Problems in Least Squares", Quarterly
     of Applied Mathematics 2(2), 1944; D. W. Marquardt, "An Algorithm for Least-Squares
     Estimation of Nonlinear Parameters", SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics 11(2), 1963).
     IK as one weighted least-squares problem over pose, rest-posture and collision costs
     follows PyRoki: C. M. Kim, B. Yi, H. Choi, Y. Ma, K. Goldberg, A. Kanazawa, "PyRoki: A
     Modular Toolkit for Robot Kinematic Optimization", IROS 2025,
     https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03728 (https://github.com/chungmin99/pyroki, MIT License,
     Copyright (c) 2025 Chung Min Kim). The approach only; no PyRoki code is used (PyRoki
     differentiates JAX code automatically, numik.rs writes the Jacobians out).
